findings.asked: Combine algebraic fractions with quadratic denominators, then use the result.
findings.wentWrong: Many did not factorise the quadratics first and ended up with cubic numerators and denominators; incorrect cancelling appeared inside the addition; a follow-through mark was available for cross-multiplying.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Factorised every quadratic, identified the lowest common denominator, combined, and cancelled only at the end.

findings.asked: Expand a product, then substitute it into a numerator and simplify a fraction.
findings.wentWrong: Gathering the terms in the numerator went wrong, and those with the right numerator often divided by 3 before factorising, producing a wrong final form.
findings.rule: Factorise the numerator before dividing anything out.

findings.asked: Simplify a fraction, then add two algebraic fractions.
findings.wentWrong: In the addition, x squared - 9 was seen as a difference of two squares but (x + 3)(x - 3) was not used as the common denominator, so cubics appeared; some cancelled terms before adding; the simplification missed a factor of 2.
findings.rule: After a difference of two squares the LCD is the pair of brackets, not the product of the denominators.

findings.asked: Combine and simplify two algebraic fractions to a constant.
findings.wentWrong: Most reached 5 of 7 marks; the killer error was subtracting a bracketed product and changing only its first term's sign; brackets dropped; premature cancelling; stopping before the final value.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Kept the subtracted product in brackets, expanded it in full, applied the minus to every term, collected, factorised and cancelled to the final value.
findings.rule: Minus a bracket: every term changes sign.

ruleToRemember: Factorise every numerator and denominator; the LCD is the product of the distinct factors; keep subtracted numerators in brackets and distribute the sign; cancel only whole factors, and simplify to the end.
aStarSignal: An addition where the LCD comes from a difference of two squares and the numerator must be subtracted with a sign change on every term, finishing as a single simplified expression.
